# 04 - What Users Hate

## The honest answer: very little, and not what was expected

This phase set out to find dissatisfaction. What it found instead is a market with
**no recorded user dissatisfaction at all** and a review corpus in which the
complaints that do exist are almost entirely requests for *more*.

## The actual complaint pattern

Across 24 usable records:

| Pattern | Example | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| **Too many options** | "having too many modules creates confusion at times" | Buyers want restraint |
| **Cannot find things** | "Some of the features can be displayed at a more visible location" | Navigation, not capability |
| **No documentation** | "No User manual!! I have been requesting this from more than 18 months" | Undersold onboarding |
| **Reach failure** | "startups wont access emails or goes to spam... SMS/whatsapp integration" | Channel gap |
| **Occasional breakage** | "Glitches occur sometimes which disrupts work" | Trust cost, not churn |
| **Wish for AI** | "they should leverage AI, enabling users to get customised deeper insights" | One reviewer, one ask |

Not one of these is a replacement trigger. Every one is additive.

## The three findings that do carry strategic weight

### 1. The displaced incumbent is not a vendor

Two Accubate reviewers name **Google Forms**. The Envisio reviewer names
**spreadsheets**. No named vendor appears in any retrieved switching field.

![Real incumbent](../_exports/charts/phase11/p11_05_real_incumbent.png)

The tool every operator actually uses costs nothing. StartupHub does not displace
AcceleratorApp - it displaces a shared drive. That reframes the competitive question
entirely: the fight is not over features, it is over **institutional defensibility**
- audit trails, committee defensibility, accreditation evidence - which is a
procurement argument, not a product argument.

### 2. The pain is operational risk, not dissatisfaction

The most credible institutional voice in the corpus is ICUBE (University of
Toronto), which evaluated AcceleratorApp and F6S and rejected both. Its stated
reasons were fragmentation, error-proneness and scale.

That is not a software complaint. It is a **dean's risk** - what happens when the
person who understood the spreadsheet leaves, and when a NIRF or IIC return has to
be reconstructed from email.

Note the recurrence of this specific failure in vendor marketing: EcoSync describes
what happens when *"the program manager changes and the previous one's spreadsheets
are on a laptop that has left, the centre loses its history."* Vendors keep
describing this because it keeps being true.

### 3. Inertia is the unclaimed gap

A vendor describing university incubation software elsewhere in this research
observed that programmes which have the means to automate still do it by hand
*"because of inertia"*.

Nobody in this category sells change management, adoption support or migration off
spreadsheets. It is the one gap that no vendor's feature page claims and no reviewer
complains about - because **the people who feel it never go looking for software in
the first place.**

That is the classic null-result trap: the absence of complaints about a gap is not
evidence the gap is absent. It is evidence the affected users are not in the
funnel.

## What this phase refuses to claim

- Not that the products are good. Only that nobody has recorded being harmed.
- Not that fragmentation is proven in India specifically. The institutional voice is
  Canadian; the user reviews are Indian but describe the same shape.
- Not that the 40-review IdeaScale base is a signal. It is 40 reviews of an
  enterprise innovation platform, not of an incubator management tool.
- Not that `NO_COMPLAINT_RECORDED` means satisfied. It means nobody wrote anything
  down.
